title: Generalist Graph Anomaly Detection via Prototype-Based Distillation
one_liner: A single detector learns to spot broken or unusual nodes in any graph by copying what normal looks like from a frozen pre-trained teacher, without needing any labels.
lead: Most graph anomaly detection methods (finding nodes that do not belong in a network) need labeled examples of broken nodes to train. This new method learns what normal looks like instead — by copying that knowledge from a pre-trained teacher that has already learned patterns across many graphs. It can then detect anomalies on brand-new graphs with zero labels and zero examples to learn from.

paras: Today's graph anomaly detectors (systems that find unusual nodes in networks) need one of two things: either a lot of labeled examples showing what broken looks like, or at least a few examples at the moment you want to use it. But in real life, anomalies are rare and expensive to label. And different graphs (a social network, a computer network, a citation graph) have completely different normal patterns.

A beginner would say: train a single detector on labeled data from one graph and try it on another. It breaks, because what normal looks like in a social network does not carry over to a power grid. The detector has memorized the shape of normal in the first graph, not the underlying principle.

callout.html: The method learns what normal looks like in any graph by distilling (copying a simplified version of) knowledge from a frozen pre-trained teacher, so it needs no labels and works on unseen graphs.

steps.text: Start with a graph neural network pre-trained on self-supervised tasks (learning from unlabeled data).
Create a student model with two branches: one shared across all graphs and one lightweight per-graph branch.
Train the student to output the same activations (internal numbers) as the teacher, using only unlabeled data from the graph.
Find clusters of normal nodes in the shared prototype space (a learned representation of what normal looks like).
On a new graph, flag nodes that sit far from the learned normal clusters and depart from the student predictions.

paras: The paper swaps the training target: instead of learning to predict labels (which are scarce), the student model learns to match the frozen teacher's hidden layer outputs. This pivot makes training feasible without labels.

hidden.name: How far the student drifts from the teacher
paras: Distillation bias is the gap between what the frozen teacher outputs and what the student produces. When a student mimics a teacher, it does not learn perfectly — it drifts. On a node the teacher saw before (during pre-training), the student and teacher agree closely. On a node in a new graph the teacher never saw, the student drifts more.

The paper uses this drift as a signal: when drift is high, the node is anomalous, because the student had to invent an output without the teacher's guidance. When drift is low, the node looks normal, because the student could follow the teacher's pattern.

heat.caption: Darker means lower distillation bias (student mimics teacher well). Lighter means higher bias (student drifts).

reads.html: When the student runs on a node, does it produce the same numbers as the teacher? If yes, normal. If no, anomalous.
Distillation bias is measured as the divergence (difference) between teacher and student outputs in the prototype space, used as an anomaly score during zero-shot detection.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: The teaching principle
paras: A frozen pre-trained teacher has already learned, during self-supervised pre-training on many graphs, to extract patterns from unlabeled node features and graph structure — patterns that show what normal looks like across diverse networks.

When a student tries to copy the teacher's outputs, it learns to extract similar patterns — but only on the parts of the graph it sees during training. On anomalies (nodes so broken or rare that they did not appear in pre-training), the student cannot follow the teacher's pattern, so it invents a different output. That invented output is the distillation bias.

The paper further aligns teacher and student in a shared prototype space (a learned coordinate system where normal nodes sit in tight clusters). This coordinate system is learned from the training graph but generalizes to new graphs, because the teacher's pre-trained patterns are already general. When you run the student on a new graph, any node far from the learned normal clusters or far from what the teacher would output is flagged as anomalous.

stages.s: Student tries to copy the teacher

math.words: The student is trained to minimize the squared difference between its own output and the teacher's output, summed across all nodes. The stronger the mismatch (the bigger the difference), the higher the loss, and the student nudges its weights to shrink that mismatch.
symbols: the total distillation loss (how far the student is from the teacher)
the hidden layer numbers the student produces for one node
the hidden layer numbers the frozen teacher produces for the same node
add up the squared differences across every node in the graph

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose teacher outputs [0.8, 0.5] for node A, student outputs [0.7, 0.6].
Now suppose teacher outputs [0.8, 0.5] for an anomaly node B, but student outputs [0.2, 0.9].
Same number of weights, but the anomalous node produces 26 times higher loss because the student cannot match the teacher.

math.note: During training, the student learns to shrink this loss, so it mimics the teacher on normal nodes. On test graphs, high distillation loss flags anomalies.

charts.title: Old method: Supervised learning
rows: Works only on seen graph type
charts.note: Must collect expensive labels and retrains for each new graph.

charts.title: This paper: Prototype-based distillation
charts.note: Teacher pre-training is done once; student distillation is label-free and transfers broadly.

items.b: Teacher did not see the anomaly type.
items.html: If the pre-training data never included a certain kind of broken node, the teacher learned no pattern for it. The student cannot distill what does not exist. The detector will miss those anomalies.

items.b: Anomalies are not visually different from normal.
items.html: If a broken node has the same feature values and neighbors as a normal node, the teacher and student will both output the same numbers. No distillation bias, no detection.
The per-graph lightweight branch can memorize noise in the training graph, making the distillation bias unreliable on new graphs with different noise patterns.
The pre-training captures diverse normal patterns, the shared branch learns what generalizes, and the personalized branch stays small enough to avoid overfitting.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a mini graph anomaly detection experiment: take a labeled graph (e.g. a social network or citation graph with marked anomalies), use a frozen pre-trained graph neural network as the teacher, train a lightweight student to distill its outputs on the unlabeled nodes, then test on held-out anomalies from a different graph. Measure how many anomalies the distillation bias catches, and compare to a supervised baseline.
demo.metric_eq: Anomaly detection rate = (True anomalies found) / (Total anomalies in test graph)
demo.closing: The demo must show that zero-shot detection (training on graph A, testing on graph B with no retraining) catches more anomalies than a method trained without distillation, because the teacher's pre-trained patterns generalize across graphs in ways that scratch-learned features do not.
